text.p: Austria's chancellor-in-waiting Viktor Klima went to ground on Sunday sparking a frenzied media hunt that turned up few fresh trails and left newspaper hounds baying in vain for an interview.
Klima became the nation's hottest topic on Saturday when Chancellor Franz Vranitzky announced his resignation after almost 11 years and named him as his chosen successor.
Senior Social Democrats swiftly endorsed the decision.

Since then the 49-year-old finance minister, who is normally anything but media shy, has not been seen in public. Only a reporter with Austrian state radio struck it lucky on Saturday by nabbing Klima on his car phone.
Asked whether he would accept Vranitzky's job, Klima replied: "I guess I'm going to do it." Then the line went dead.

Messages left at Klima's home went unanswered over the weekend and calls to some of his favourite haunts failed to locate him. Sources at the finance ministry avoided the media probes and party colleagues said they knew nothing of Klima's whereabouts.

Vranitzky revealed that he and his wife Christine had dined with Klima and his wife Sonja on Saturday evening to discuss the way forward. "He will probably hold a news conference in two days' time," Vranitzky said.

In the coming week Klima will outline his policies to Social Democratic Party leaders and will probably choose his ministerial line-up, appointing a new finance minister and possibly carrying out a wide-ranging reshuffle.

Possible departures could include Women's Minister Helga Konrad, Social Affairs Minister Franz Hums and Transport Minister Rudolf Scholten, political commentators said. Though Scholten was also mooted as a possible finance minister.
The conservative People's Party, junior partner in the coalition government, appeared irritated by what it considered a Social Democrat attempt to shut it out of decision-making.

People's Party leader and Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel complained that he was among the last to learn of Vranitzky's resignation and he insisted his party wanted a say in the choice of finance minister.
"We want to make our thoughts known and we do not want to find out (who has been chosen) via the media," Schuessel said.
By Sunday afternoon only one Social Democrat ministerial post was fixed. Party business manager Brigitte Ederer said that Klima had asked her to stay on and she had agreed.
A pre-recorded interview with Klima, broadcast on Austrian radio on Sunday morning, showed what a fast-moving business politics can be.
"I never had any political ambitions. I see myself leaving politics in a few years and maybe living on a little farm with my wife. We both love animals," he said.
